passage: My neighbour Keerthana, twenty-six, has a three-year-old daughter, Ira, and I've watched how she handles questions about faith. Last week Ira came out of the lift carrying a paper diya from nursery and asked, "Is God in the diya?" Keerthana didn't laugh. She said, "Some people believe God is everywhere, some believe in different gods, and some believe there is no God. Which story would you like first?" Ira chose the elephant one. Later I saw a shelf in their hall with picture books: Diwali, Eid, Christmas, and one about stars for people who don't pray. I can't say what Keerthana herself believes; she never said. But I've heard her tell Ira, "You can ask anyone anything, politely." Minakshi

qa.q: What did Ira ask when she came out of the lift?
qa.a: Ira asked, "Is God in the diya?"

qa.q: What might Minakshi be feeling as the neighbour watches how Keerthana answers?
qa.a: Minakshi seems impressed and thoughtful, though Minakshi can only guess what Keerthana herself believes.

qa.q: Which choice by Keerthana shows fairness to many beliefs?
qa.a: Keerthana answered that some believe God is everywhere, some believe in different gods and some believe there is no God, and offered Ira a choice of stories.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see her daughter's questions?
qa.a: As welcome and worth answering calmly. She tells Ira to ask anyone anything, politely, so curiosity is safe.

grounding: A parent decides to raise a child with knowledge of several faiths and non-belief, presenting each fairly and welcoming the child's questions.

passage: Tuesday. Lalremsiami noticed four-year-old Zoe humming the hymns she had heard from her grandmother. That evening Lalremsiami told Wasim, "She asked about Eid too. I want her to know both, and also that some people don't pray at all." Wasim nodded. "Let's tell each story fairly, and let her ask." Saturday. They bought picture books on Christmas, Eid and Diwali, and one about how people wonder about the stars. Wasim read the Eid one, Lalremsiami the Christmas one. Zoe asked, "Which is the true one?" They looked at each other. "Different families believe different things," Wasim said. "You can ask us anything." Thursday. Zoe told her teacher, "My Papa's Eid and my Mama's Christmas. And Ravi's Diwali." She sounded proud.

qa.q: What kinds of picture books did they buy on Saturday?
qa.a: They bought picture books on Christmas, Eid and Diwali, and one about how people wonder about the stars.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami be feeling as the plan for Zoe is put to Wasim?
qa.a: Lalremsiami is hopeful and a little careful, wanting Zoe to know both traditions and also that some people don't pray at all.

qa.q: Which choice did Lalremsiami and Wasim make when Zoe asked which is the true one?
qa.a: They looked at each other and answered that different families believe different things and that Zoe can ask anything, instead of choosing one story.

qa.q: How might Zoe have felt telling her teacher about Eid, Christmas and Diwali?
qa.a: Proud and included, since she sounded proud when listing her Papa's Eid, her Mama's Christmas and Ravi's Diwali.

grounding: A parent decides how to raise a child with knowledge of several faiths and non-belief, presenting each fairly and letting the child ask.

passage:
Sonali, you asked why your father knows so much about every religion. It was my doing. Sit.
I was twenty-five, a young mother in a railway colony, and your father was six. One day he came home from school crying because a boy said his friend Yusuf would "go to hell." He asked me, "Is that true, Ma?"
I didn't know how to answer. My family said only our way was right. So I decided: I would teach him about every faith fairly, and about people who believe in none.
Every Sunday, we read one story: from the Gita, the Bible, the Quran, the Guru Granth Sahib, the Buddha, and one about a scientist who didn't believe. He asked questions; I answered honestly, or said I didn't know.
At fourteen, he defended that same Yusuf in a fight at school. That was when I knew it had worked. Your Parul Dadi was right to try.

qa.q: What did the boy at school say about Yusuf?
qa.a: A boy said Yusuf would "go to hell."

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when her son asked if it was true?
qa.a: Parul felt unsure and unsettled, not knowing how to answer and not satisfied with her family's view.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Parul's story?
qa.a: It was her decision to teach her son about every faith and non-belief fairly, reading stories each Sunday and answering his questions honestly.

qa.q: How did the teaching affect Parul's son as a boy?
qa.a: It made him respectful and brave, so at fourteen he defended Yusuf at school.

grounding: An elder recalls deciding as a young mother to teach her son about many faiths and non-belief fairly, letting him ask questions, which made him respectful.

passage:
It was nine at night, Shreya had a work call at six the next morning, and her daughter, six, still wouldn't sleep.
"Mumma, why does Afreen Aunty's family pray five times? And why don't we?"
Shreya, twenty-six, was exhausted. She almost said, "Just go to sleep." Then she remembered her own mother, who had answered every question about other faiths with "Don't ask."
She sat back down on the bed. "Afreen Aunty is Muslim. They pray five times a day because they believe it keeps them close to God. We're Hindu, and we pray differently. And some people, like Papa's friend Tom, don't believe in God at all."
"Who is right?"
"People believe different things, and they're all trying to be good. You can ask Afreen Aunty tomorrow; she'd like that."
Her daughter yawned. "And Tom Uncle too?"
"And Tom Uncle too."

qa.q: How many times a day does Afreen Aunty's family pray?
qa.a: Afreen Aunty's family prays five times a day.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she almost said "Just go to sleep"?
qa.a: Shreya felt exhausted and pressed for time, but remembered how her own mother shut down questions and chose patience.

qa.q: What in Shreya's answer builds respect?
qa.a: She described each belief fairly, including non-belief, and invited her daughter to ask Afreen Aunty and Tom Uncle herself.

qa.q: How might Shreya's daughter see Afreen Aunty after this talk?
qa.a: The child might feel curious and friendly toward Afreen Aunty, seeing her prayers as interesting rather than strange.

grounding: Though tired and short on time, a parent answers her child's questions about another faith and non-belief fairly, building informed respect.

passage:
Irfan and his wife had agreed on almost everything before their son was born, except this.
Now Ojas was five, and at his grandparents' houses he heard two different answers about God. Irfan's mother taught him the Kalma. His wife's mother taught him the Gayatri mantra. Ojas came home and asked, "Which one is mine?"
Irfan, twenty-six, sat on the balcony that night with his wife. "I don't want him to feel he has to choose to please one of them," he said. She agreed.
So they made a small plan: stories from both faiths, and from others too; honest answers to every question; and permission to say, "I'm not sure yet."
The next morning Ojas asked, "Is Nana-ji's God angry with Dadi's God?"
Irfan laughed and pulled him close. "No. People just pray in different ways. Ask me anything, anytime."

qa.q: What did Irfan's mother teach Ojas?
qa.a: Irfan's mother taught him the Kalma.

qa.q: What was Irfan worried about on the balcony?
qa.a: Irfan was worried that Ojas would feel he had to choose a faith to please one set of grandparents.

qa.q: Why is Irfan and his wife's plan a good one?
qa.a: Presenting several faiths fairly, answering questions honestly and allowing "I'm not sure yet" helps Ojas grow into an informed, respectful adult.

qa.q: What is it like for Ojas to hear two answers about God?
qa.a: Ojas seems confused and a little worried, asking which one is his and whether the gods are angry with each other.

grounding: A parent in an interfaith family plans to teach his son about several faiths fairly and let him ask questions, so he can grow up informed and respectful.

passage:
"Papa, Kabir in my class says only his God is real. Is he right?"
Vishal looked at Salma over Aarav's head.
"What do you think, jaan?" asked Salma, his mother.
"I don't know. Dadi says Krishna. Nani says Allah."
"Both of them believe with their whole hearts," Vishal said. "Some people believe in many gods, some in one, and some, like Uncle Joseph next door, in none."
"Uncle Joseph doesn't have a God?"
"No. And he's the one who fixed your cycle," Salma said.
"So who's right?"
"People have asked that forever," Vishal said. "We'll read stories from all of them, and you can keep asking. Any question, any time."
Later, clearing the plates, Salma said quietly, "I was scared he'd feel pulled in two." Vishal nodded. "Maybe he'll feel he has more to learn from."

qa.q: Who fixed Aarav's cycle?
qa.a: Uncle Joseph, who believes in no God, fixed it.

qa.q: What was Salma worried about, and when does it show?
qa.a: Salma was scared Aarav would feel pulled in two between the family's faiths, which she admits quietly while clearing the plates.

qa.q: How could these parents keep teaching fairly as Aarav grows?
qa.a: They can keep reading stories from each faith and from non-belief side by side, and keep answering any question without naming a winner.

qa.q: How might Aarav experience his parents' answer?
qa.a: Aarav probably feels reassured and curious rather than confused, since both Dadi's and Nani's beliefs are treated with respect and he is invited to keep asking.

grounding: It illustrates parents choosing to present several faiths and non-belief fairly and inviting their child's questions.
